title: Berkley Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Berkley-area wells have a 28 ft median depth, but monitoring wells dominate the records. Review yields, water levels, costs and buyer risks.
h1: What Berkley Well Records Mean for Your Property
intro_html:
A shallow well record near Berkley is not necessarily a household water supply. Within 5 miles, Colorado DWR records show 11,991 permitted wells, but 64% are classified for monitoring and only 16% for domestic or household use. That distinction matters when you compare depths or price a new well.

The area’s recorded median depth is 28 feet. Treat that as a starting point for research, not a drilling specification. For property in Berkley or nearby Twin Lakes, Lakeside and North Washington, the useful comparison is a neighboring well with the same intended use and aquifer.

sections.heading: Why Berkley’s 28-Foot Median Needs Context
sections.html:
Of the 6,721 wells reporting depth, the median is 28 feet and the middle half fall between 20 and 40 feet. That is a shallow record set: 90% are under 100 feet. Yet the deepest recorded well reaches 1,751 feet, so shallow construction is not the only possibility here.

Permits include Alluvial and Quaternary Alluvium aquifer labels, while the local drilling cost model assumes Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. A driller needs to establish the actual target formation and permitted use before bidding. The 20–40-foot range describes the middle of these records; with monitoring wells dominating, it is not a dependable depth allowance for a new household supply.

sections.heading: Reported Yields Look Useful, but Household Comparisons Matter
sections.html:
The 275 records with reported pump yields have a median of 13.0 gpm, with the middle half between 8.0 and 40.0 gpm. Those rates can look encouraging for a buyer, but a reported pumping rate does not establish sustained household performance or the amount you are legally allowed to pump.

At the low end, 6% report under 1 gpm and 8% report 1–5 gpm. A low-producing well may require storage and careful demand management; it deserves a sustained pumping test before purchase. Ask for recovery observations as well as yield. The limited yield reporting and mixed well uses make it especially important to compare domestic wells rather than assume every nearby record represents a usable home supply.

sections.heading: Water Is Often Shallow in the Berkley Records
sections.html:
Static water level is the resting depth to water, not the drilled depth or the available pumping supply. Among 272 reporting wells, the median is 10 feet below ground and the middle half is 7–16 feet.

The decade medians move from 32 feet in the 1960s to 12 feet in the 2010s and 8 feet in the 2020s. Those figures do not show a dropping water table: later measurements are shallower. They also do not prove that water levels rose at a particular property, because the measurements can represent different wells and aquifers. Shallow groundwater is a reason to investigate excavation, foundation and septic conditions, not evidence that a household well will produce reliably.

sections.heading: Berkley’s Permit History Is Heavily Monitoring-Oriented
sections.html:
Permit activity increased from 508 records in the 1980s to 2,234 in the 1990s. The 2010s account for 2,934 permits, and the 2020s account for 1,081, with the newest permit dated 2025. Do not treat the current decade as a completed period or these counts as a measure of new homes.

Only 5,934 records are marked constructed. The most frequent driller-field entry is “Authorized (Pe, Pg)” with 4,109 records; that label should not be treated as a conventional drilling-company recommendation. Other leading entries are Layne, Christensen Co. (Tormoehlen, David A.) with 210 and Ground Exploration Llc (Bender, Joseph T.) with 207. Their presence documents historical work, not current availability or household-well specialization.

sections.heading: Budgeting Beyond a Shallow Drilled Hole in Berkley
sections.html:
The supplied Denver Basin sedimentary-bedrock cost model uses $50–$70 per foot. At the recorded median depth of 28 feet, that puts the drilled hole at about $1,400–$2,000. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at about $7,400–$14,000.

That is a planning estimate, not a household-well quote. Monitoring wells strongly influence the median depth, and a permitted domestic target may be different. Have the contractor separate drilling, casing and grout, pump equipment, electrical work and trenching in the bid. Confirm assumptions about access and the proposed aquifer. Water treatment, difficult site conditions and a different completion depth should be discussed rather than assumed covered by the median-based estimate.

sections.heading: Environmental Records Make Testing Important Here
sections.html:
Within about 10 miles of Berkley, the mapped inventory includes 703 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 191 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites and 6 historic mine features. These are screening flags, not proof that a particular well is contaminated. A sampling location is not automatically a confirmed contamination source.

Review the closest relevant sites, the well’s screened interval and available groundwater reports before choosing a laboratory testing panel. Ask about PFAS testing alongside routine household-water testing. Inspect casing, seals and surface drainage. Low yield remains a separate concern: 6% of reported yields are under 1 gpm. A nearby completed well does not guarantee a productive hole on your lot, and shallow groundwater can complicate septic siting and foundation excavation.

sections.heading: Before Buying a Berkley Lot, Match the Records to the Plan
sections.html:
Start with the parcel’s water-service options and DWR permit status, not the nearest dot on the map. An exempt household-use permit is not blanket permission for irrigation or other uses. Depending on the source and proposed use, augmentation requirements may need review.

Then compare constructed domestic wells in the same aquifer around Berkley, Twin Lakes or Sherrelwood. Obtain the seller’s permit, completion report, pump-test results and water-quality results. Have a driller review any missing information before you commit. For a building lot, coordinate the well location with access, the house footprint, utilities and an approved septic layout where applicable. Resolve legal supply, tested performance and site feasibility before relying on the area’s shallow median depth.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Berkley, Colorado?
faq.a: Within 5 miles of Berkley, the recorded median well depth is 28 feet, and the middle half range from 20 to 40 feet. However, 64% of permits are for monitoring. A new household well should be planned from its permitted aquifer and comparable domestic completion reports, not the overall shallow median.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Berkley?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $50–$70 per foot for Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At the 28-foot median depth, the hole alone is about $1,400–$2,000, while a finished system is about $7,400–$14,000. Because monitoring wells dominate the records, confirm the household well’s target depth before using that estimate as a budget.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Berkley?
faq.a: The median reported pump yield is 13.0 gpm, with the middle half between 8.0 and 40.0 gpm. Only 275 records report yield, and 6% of those report under 1 gpm. For a purchase, obtain a sustained pumping test and recovery observations; the area median does not establish your well’s performance or permitted use.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Berkley, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from a permit or depth record. The surrounding inventory includes 703 PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles, but that does not establish contamination at your property. Review relevant nearby environmental reports and have the actual well water tested, including discussion of PFAS with the laboratory.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Berkley?
faq.a: The supplied records do not show a dropping water table. Median measured depth to water was 32 feet in the 1960s, 12 feet in the 2010s and 8 feet in the 2020s. Later measurements are shallower, but different wells and aquifers may be represented. These figures cannot establish a trend for an individual household well.
